query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of aluminum (~5–10 at%) to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy, followed by an aging heat treatment to induce coherent gamma prime precipitates, will improve the alloy’s elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the same alloy without aluminum.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy that meets the compositional definition (with each principal element between 5 and 35 at%) and is presently a homogeneous solid solution (without deliberate gamma prime precipitate formation).
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled aluminum addition (around 5–10 at% as a minor constituent) into the alloy composition, then apply an aging heat treatment under conditions optimized to promote the nucleation and growth of coherent gamma prime precipitates.
generation.conditions: Both the modified (with Al) and control (without Al) alloys are synthesized under identical processing conditions. The aging heat treatment is applied at a controlled temperature and duration (values defined by process optimization) such that gamma prime phase precipitation is achieved. Elevated-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., high-temperature yield strength and creep tests) are conducted under service-relevant conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and dispersion of coherent gamma prime precipitates within the solid-solution matrix.
generation.mechanism: The gamma prime precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thereby increasing creep resistance and yield strength by impeding plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced elevated-temperature mechanical properties—specifically, higher yield strength and improved creep resistance—relative to the control alloy, as a result of precipitation strengthening via the gamma prime phase.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without any aluminum addition and without a heat-treatment step designed to induce gamma prime precipitates.
generation.boundary: All constituent element concentrations remain within the 5–35 at% range. The aluminum addition level is kept low enough to promote gamma prime formation without destabilizing the overall single-phase microstructure; the aging temperature and time are selected to avoid overcoarsening or formation of unwanted secondary phases.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimum aluminum content and the detailed aging parameters for maximum gamma prime precipitation efficacy are not predetermined and require experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set with the controlled aluminum addition (5–10 at%) and the other as the unmodified control. Process both identically, then subject them to the same aging heat treatment optimized for gamma prime phase formation. Characterize the microstructure using TEM and XRD to confirm the presence (or absence) of gamma prime precipitates and measure their size and distribution. Finally, perform elevated-temperature mechanical tests (such as yield strength and creep tests) under identical service-relevant conditions.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (presence, volume fraction, and distribution of gamma prime precipitates via TEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-added alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the control, or if microstructural analysis shows no evidence of gamma prime precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most intensely investigated HEA systems, primarily forming cubic phases is AlCoCrCuFeNi [,]. Due to the positive enthalpy of mixing ∆Hmix among Cu and the elements Fe and Cr, segregation was observed, deteriorating mechanical and corrosion properties. Therefore, subsequent investigations focused on the copper-free derivative AlCoCrFeNi [,,,,]. Early studies concentrated on the equimolar composition. However, investigations showed that optimum properties are usually achieved when choosing a differing chemical composition []. Investigating the influence of different alloying elements showed a strong influence of aluminium on the microstructure, phase composition, and properties [,]. For a low aluminium content, fcc phases are stabilised, whereas high contents of aluminium act as a strong bcc phase stabiliser [,]. In addition, the formation of complex phases can be suppressed for a high aluminium content []. Furthermore, the influence of additional alloying elements has been investigated.
